blocks.text: Filtration separates one component of a two-component heterogeneous mixture from a solution. First a suitable solvent is chosen in which one component dissolves completely while the other remains practically insoluble. For a mixture of common salt and sand, the mixture is dissolved in distilled water: the salt distributes itself throughout the water to give a homogeneous mixture, a solution of common salt in water, while the sand remains undissolved and settles. The salt is the solute and the water the solvent, the solvent being the component present in excess. Filtration then separates the sand.

blocks.alt: A hand pours a liquid mixture from a tilted beaker down a glass rod into a glass funnel lined with filter paper. The funnel is held by a clamp on a stand, and drops of filtrate fall into a beaker below.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.1: The process of filtration (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.1).

blocks.title: Solute, solvent, solution, filtrate and residue
blocks.text: In a solution the dissolved substance is the solute and the liquid in excess the solvent. After filtration the liquid collected in the flask below the funnel is the filtrate, and the solid left on the filter is the residue.

Filtration through a glass funnel and filter paper is usually slow: as the mixture is poured on, the solvent passes through, leaving the suspended particles on the paper. Filter papers come in various porosities (pore sizes), chosen according to the particle size of the precipitate; the paper should be large enough to be one-quarter to one-half full of precipitate at the end, so that the filtrate runs down the side of the beaker without splashing (Figure 15.1). The paper is folded in half, then in half again, and opened into a cone, inserted into a 60-degree funnel, moistened with water and pressed down (Figure 15.2a).

blocks.alt: Three drawings: a round filter paper with a dashed line down the middle (first fold), the half circle with a dashed line across it (second fold), and the paper opened into a cone (forming the cone).
blocks.caption: Figure 15.2a: Folding of filtration paper (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.2a).

blocks.text: The rate of filtration through a conical funnel is much increased by a fluted filter paper, folded fan-wise with alternate elevations and depressions (Figure 15.2b).

blocks.alt: Seven steps: filter disk; fold in half; fold in half again; fold to crease the quarter section; fold to crease the eight section; the pleated accordion shape; open filter cone.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.2b: Fluted filter paper (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.2b).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed caption reads 'Fluttled filter paper'; the correct word is fluted.

A precipitate can also be filtered by suction through a crucible. A Gooch crucible is porcelain with a perforated bottom covered with paper pulp or a filter paper cut to size (Figure 15.3); placed in a suction apparatus it filters quickly, and it suits precipitates that must be ignited at high temperature; with its perforations covered by an asbestos mat it can filter solutions that react with paper, such as concentrated HCl and KMnO4.

blocks.alt: A white porcelain crucible turned upside down to show its bottom full of small holes, with a loose perforated disc and a round plate beside it.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.3: Gooch crucible (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.3).

blocks.text: A sintered glass crucible has a porous glass disc sealed into the bottom and needs no preparation (Figure 15.4).

blocks.alt: A glass crucible with a white porous glass disc sealed across its lower part.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.4: Sintered glass crucible (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.4).
